The Wood frog, Lithobates sylvaticus, is a prolific breeder whose reproductive output is tightly linked to the aquatic thermal regime during the brief breeding window immediately after pond thaw. In many populations, a single gravid female can produce an egg mass containing approximately 900 eggs per breeding season, representing a substantial annual reproductive investment. Under prolonged cool spring conditions typical of northern latitudes, where water temperatures hover near 15 °C [T = 15 °C], this maximum reproductive output of approximately 2.5 eggs per day [Ri = of approximately 2.5 eggs per day] underscores the explosive, synchronous nature of their breeding aggregations. This intense pulse of oviposition is energetically demanding and is supported by the species' moderate basal metabolic demands. Respirometry trials conducted under standard laboratory conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have determined that the maximum resting metabolic rate of an adult Wood frog is 0.0179 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0179 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the physiological baseline from which reproductive and locomotory costs must be met during the active spring period.

The early life stages of Lithobates sylvaticus are characterized by a remarkably small initial size and rapid developmental progression under favorable thermal conditions. Neonates, measured immediately following eclosion from the gelatinous egg mass, possess an average wet weight of only 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a mass derived from the spherical egg which has a mean diameter of 1.7 mm. This diminutive size, comparable to that of a small grain of sand, places the hatchling at an immediate risk from desiccation and predation as it begins its aquatic larval phase. The interval between oviposition and the hatching event is relatively brief when temperatures are optimal. In eggs incubated at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the age at birth is 14 days [ab = 14 days], although lower temperatures typical of ephemeral woodland ponds in early spring can extend this period to between 10 and 14 days as metabolic rates slow. This rapid embryonic development is an adaptation to the ephemeral nature of the breeding habitat, allowing larvae to enter the water column and begin feeding before ponds potentially dry or become overcrowded with competing tadpoles.

The larval period in Wood frogs is highly plastic, a trait that allows populations to buffer against interannual variation in hydroperiod length. Field studies tracking individual tadpoles from hatching through metamorphosis have established that the time since birth at metamorphosis averages 100 days  when development proceeds at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This duration, which typically falls within the reported range of 65 to 130 days, reflects the slow, steady growth of the herbivorous tadpole as it accumulates somatic tissue and develops limb buds. The transformation itself involves a dramatic morphological reorganisation, including complete tail resorption and the transition from branchial to pulmonary respiration, culminating in the emergence of a tiny terrestrial froglet. The length of the larval stage is a critical determinant of recruitment success; individuals that accelerate their development to metamorphose earlier may escape pond desiccation but often emerge at a smaller body size, which can compromise their subsequent overwintering survival and future reproductive potential.

Following metamorphosis, the terrestrial juvenile phase represents a protracted period of growth and energy storage that precedes the attainment of sexual maturity. Female Wood frogs in particular exhibit a substantial increase in body mass during this stage, ultimately reaching an ultimate wet weight of 12.7 grams [Wwi = 12.7 grams] by the time they are fully grown adults. This mass, which is among the highest recorded for females in the species, is necessary to support the production of the large annual clutch of eggs. The journey to this adult size is a long one, governed by the same cool thermal regime that defines the species' northern range. Measurements from mark-recapture studies indicate that at a sustained environmental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since metamorphosis at puberty for females is 912 days [tp = 912 days]. This interval, equivalent to roughly two and a half years, is a period during which the juvenile must balance the demands of foraging, predator avoidance, and the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves to survive the first winter hibernation and subsequent breeding seasons.

Longevity data for Lithobates sylvaticus reveal a life history strategy that prioritizes early, intense reproduction over extended survival, a pattern common among small-bodied anurans inhabiting unpredictable temperate environments. Under natural field conditions and at a mean ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is 5 years [am = 5 years], with most individuals living considerably shorter lives due to high overwinter mortality and predation by garter snakes and avian predators. This relatively short lifespan places a premium on the reproductive success of the mature females that survive to their first breeding event. A female that reaches puberty at 912 days after metamorphosis [tp = 912 days after metamorphosis] typically has only two or three breeding seasons in which to contribute offspring to the next generation at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The combination of a high maximum daily fecundity and a brief adult life stage underscores the boom-or-bust demographic strategy that has enabled this species to dominate the amphibian community across much of its boreal and temperate North American range.
